Empirical Research Plan – Economic Consequences of Dust-Bowl Erosion  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (two–way fixed effects) complemented by an event-study.  
Why appropriate  
• 769 counties observed every Census year from 1910–1990s ⇒ rich panel.  
• Large, once-for-all shock (severe erosion) whose intensity differs sharply across counties but whose timing is common (1934–1936).  
• Erosion categories are time-invariant after 1940 (map reflects cumulative damage). Thus we can compare the change in outcomes in highly eroded counties to the change in lightly eroded counties before vs. after 1934.  
• Event-study coefficients (year-by-year interactions) will test the parallel-trend assumption and trace short- vs. long-run effects.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
ErosionHigh_i  = 1 if county i is classified “high erosion” by the Soil Conservation Service map  
ErosionMed_i   = 1 if “medium erosion” (optional second dose)  
Baseline: “low erosion” counties.

Control group  
Low-erosion counties in the same 12-state region.

Treatment timing  
Post_t = 1 for years ≥ 1934 (first Dust-Bowl drought year); 0 for years ≤ 1930.  
(Event study will interact each Census year with ErosionHigh_i.)

Running variable / cutoff  
Not applicable (not an RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the Dust Bowl, highly and lightly eroded counties would have followed similar trends in land values, revenues, etc.  
• Plausibility: Within‐state controls, similar pre-1930 cropping patterns; can be evaluated with pre-period event-study leads.

A2. No spillovers (SUTVA): Outcomes in low-erosion counties are not directly affected by neighboring high-erosion counties (e.g., through out-migration that depresses wages or land prices).  
• Plausibility: Some migration spillovers likely; we will cluster errors at the state level and show robustness to dropping adjacent counties.

A3. Erosion classification exogenous to post-1930 shocks once we condition on pre-Dust-Bowl covariates, state×year shocks, and weather.  
• Plausibility: Erosion intensity is driven mainly by pre-1930 soil characteristics and drought; we will control for 1920 crop mix and decade-specific PDSI.

A4. Stable composition of counties: County borders are fixed; agricultural‐Census sampling frames consistent across years.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential drought exposure (climate shocks correlate with erosion severity).  
• Include county-level PDSI, temperature, and precipitation controls interacted with year dummies; verify results within climatic sub-regions.  

T2. Policy response heterogeneity (AAA payments, SCS projects, New Deal spending).  
• Control for per-acre New-Deal conservation spending and AAA payments; re-estimate after dropping top/bottom New-Deal counties.  

T3. Migration-induced general-equilibrium effects (treated counties empty out, affecting control counties).  
• Spatially weight controls: drop counties within 100 km of any high-erosion county; show that coefficients are stable.  
• Estimate spatial DID with Conley-GMM standard errors.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#-------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#-------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # TWFE and event-study
library(ggplot2)
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

#-------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data (CSV assumed in working directory)
#-------------------------------------------------------------
ag   <- fread("county_ag_1910_1997.csv")        # main Ag & Pop Census panel
soil <- fread("county_soil_erosion.csv")        # erosion class
wx   <- fread("county_weather_PDSI.csv")        # PDSI & temp
newdeal <- fread("county_newdeal_spend.csv")    # AAA + SCS

#-------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge and Variable Construction
#-------------------------------------------------------------
panel <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by=c("fips","year"), all=TRUE),
                list(ag, soil, wx, newdeal))

# balance panel on 769 counties × years wanted
years.keep <- c(1910,1920,1930,1940,1950,1960,1970,1980,1990)
panel <- panel[fips %in% unique(soil$fips) & year %in% years.keep]

# Treatment dummies
panel[, erosion_high := (erosion_class=="high")]
panel[, erosion_med  := (erosion_class=="medium")]

# Post indicator
panel[, post := as.integer(year >= 1934)]

# Outcomes (examples)
panel[, ln_landvalue := log(land_value_per_acre)]
panel[, ln_agrev     := log(ag_revenue)]
panel[, ln_pop       := log(total_pop)]

# County × year climate controls
panel[, PDSI_postint := PDSI * post]

#-------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID Specification
#   y_it = β1 (erosion_high_i × post_t) + β2 X_it + μ_i + τ_t + ε_it
#-------------------------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(ln_landvalue ~ erosion_high:post + 
                                    erosion_med:post + 
                                    PDSI + temp + 
                                    newdeal_spend |
                                    fips + year,
                  data = panel, cluster = ~state)

summary(did_main)

#-------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-Study using SUN & AB estimator
#-------------------------------------------------------------
panel[, treat_year := 1934]              # same adoption date for all treated
es  <- feols(ln_landvalue ~ sunab(treat_year, year, ref.p = -2) |
                               fips + year,
             data = panel[erosion_high==1 | erosion_class=="low"],
             cluster = ~state)

iplot(es, ref.line = 0, xlab="Years relative to 1934", ylab="Log land value")

#-------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: add county-specific linear trends
#-------------------------------------------------------------
panel[, time_trend := year - 1910]
did_trend <- feols(ln_landvalue ~ erosion_high:post + erosion_med:post + 
                                     PDSI + temp + newdeal_spend |
                                     fips + year + fips*time_trend,
                   data = panel, cluster = ~state)
summary(did_trend)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts topsoil loss lowers productivity of cropland, reducing land values and crop revenue; some adjustment through shifting land to pasture and out-migration.  
Priors (orders of magnitude):  
• Short-run (1940) β̂ ≈ −0.20 log points (≈-18%) for land values in high-erosion counties.  
• Partial recovery over decades, but long-run (1970-1990) still −0.05 to −0.10 log points.  
• Cropland acreage falls 10–15 p.p.; pasture increases 5–8 p.p.; population declines 8–12%.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: No differential pre-trends (lead coefficients ≈ 0)           – 0.8  
C2: Treatment exogenous conditional on controls                 – 0.7  
C3: No spillovers / SUTVA                                       – 0.6  
C4: Stable outcome measurement across time                      – 1.0  
C5: Robustness across alternative specs & samples               – 0.9  

Average ≈ 0.8 – credible but not bullet-proof.
